topic_title: The Supermarket Shuffle: Why Shelves Keep Moving

sources.title: Altering product placement to create a healthier layout in supermarkets: Outcomes on store sales, customer purchasing, and diet in a prospective matched controlled cluster study
sources.authors_or_organization: Vogel, C., Crozier, S., Penn-Newman, D., Ball, K., Moon, G., Lord, J., Cooper, C., Baird, J.
sources.fetched_extraction: A prospective matched controlled pilot cluster study across 6 discount supermarkets in England (3 intervention, 3 matched control), running April 2016 to March 2017 (6 months). Intervention had two parts: (1) expanding fresh fruit and vegetable sections and repositioning them near store entrances, plus relocating frozen vegetables to more prominent aisles; (2) removing confectionery from all checkouts and from aisle-end displays directly opposite checkouts, replacing them with nonfood items and water. Findings: fresh fruit and vegetable sales rose by 1.71 standard deviations at 3 months (95% CI 0.45-2.96, P=0.01), equivalent to approximately 6,170 extra portions per store per week, and by 2.42 SDs at 6 months (95% CI 0.22-4.62, P=0.03), approximately 9,820 extra portions per store per week. Confectionery sales fell by 1.05 SDs at 3 months (95% CI -1.98 to -0.12, P=0.03), approximately 1,359 fewer portions per store per week, and by 1.37 SDs at 6 months (95% CI -2.95 to 0.22, P=0.09, not statistically significant), approximately 1,575 fewer portions per store per week. No significant impact was detected on overall total store sales in any period. Among 150 women recruited to a linked purchasing/diet survey (62 intervention, 88 control; 8% attrition at 3 months, 14% at 6 months), women's self-reported diet quality improved at 3 months in intervention stores (beta=0.29 SDs, P=0.04, unadjusted), and fruit/vegetable purchasing increased in intervention households while decreasing in control households; confectionery purchasing showed no significant intervention effect.

sources.title: Exploring the Impact of Supermarket Store Layout and Atmospheric Elements on Consumer Behavior: A Field Research Study in Greece
sources.authors_or_organization: Mantratzis, P., Tsiotras, G., Tsironis, L.K., Gotzamani, K.
sources.journal_or_venue: Journal of Operations and Strategic Planning (SAGE / International Management Institute, Kolkata)
sources.fetched_extraction: A field research study of 205 participants in Greece assessing shopper perceptions and attitudes toward supermarket layout and atmospheric elements (building design, customer traffic patterns, merchandise arrangement, spatial proximity). The study reports that retail environment characteristics impact shoppers' emotional reactions, which in turn influence impulse buying behavior, and that store atmosphere and layout design significantly influence consumer decision-making, perception of the store, and satisfaction. Note: only abstract/summary-level detail was accessible via direct fetch; full-text methodology and effect-size figures were not retrievable.
